passage:
It was class photo day, and the monsoon had turned Noor's hair into a frizzy cloud on the walk to school. There was no time to go home, and the photographer was already setting up in the quad.
Noor stood in the second row, certain the whole class was staring. Every whisper sounded like "Look at that hair." When Thomas leaned across and said something, Noor snapped, "I know, okay? I know it looks awful."
Thomas blinked. "I said your shoelace is untied."
Noor looked around. Most people were fixing their own collars or squinting into the sun. The harsh words Noor had been hearing all morning had sounded like everyone else's. They were Noor's own.

qa.q: What did Thomas actually say to Noor?
qa.a: "I said your shoelace is untied."

qa.q: Why did every whisper sound to Noor like 'Look at that hair'?
qa.a: Noor already felt self-conscious and embarrassed about the frizz, so that private criticism seemed to be coming from everyone else 😰

qa.q: What turning point showed Noor what was really happening?
qa.a: Thomas's reply about the shoelace made Noor look around and see people busy with their own collars, not staring.

qa.q: How might Thomas feel after being snapped at?
qa.a: Thomas is probably startled and a little stung, having only tried to help with a shoelace.

grounding: On a rainy photo day a teenager unsure about their hair hears their own harsh thoughts as the whole class's judgement.

passage:
Aditi got her new glasses on Saturday, thick black frames, and by Monday she was sure the whole of Class 9B in her Kolkata school had noticed. In the corridor she kept her head down. When two boys laughed near the water cooler, her cheeks burned; they had to be laughing at her face.
At lunch she told Ishita, "Everyone thinks I look like an owl. I can tell."
Ishita put down her roti. "Who said that?"
"No one said it. They just think it."
"Aditi, those boys were laughing at a cricket video. And I think the frames suit you."
Aditi pushed the glasses up her nose. She wasn't sure she believed it. But she looked at the boys again.

qa.q: What were the two boys actually laughing at?
qa.a: A cricket video.

qa.q: Why is Aditi sure everyone thinks she looks like an owl?
qa.a: Aditi is unsure about the new glasses herself, so her own harsh thoughts feel like the whole class's opinion.

qa.q: Which question from Ishita helped test Aditi's belief?
qa.a: Asking "Who said that?" pushed Aditi to notice that nobody had, a useful check to borrow whenever the feeling comes back.

qa.q: What might Ishita feel as her friend puts herself down?
qa.a: Ishita may feel a bit sad and frustrated that Aditi can't see what Ishita sees: frames that suit her.

grounding: A fourteen-year-old with new glasses believes her whole class is mocking her, until a friend asks who actually said it.

passage:
"I'm not going to the farewell."
"Why? You were excited last week." Chetan looked up from his phone.
"Look at my face, bhaiya. This spot. Everyone in class will stare at it all night."
"Saurabh. It's one spot."
"You don't get it. They already think I'm ugly. Every time someone looks at me in class, I know what they're thinking."
Chetan was quiet for a moment. "What are they thinking?"
"That I'm gross."
"Who's thinking it? Them, or you?"
Saurabh opened his mouth, then shut it.
"I had the same fear at your age," Chetan said. "Turned out nobody was looking. They were all worried about their own faces."

qa.q: What event is Saurabh refusing to go to?
qa.a: The farewell.

qa.q: Why is Saurabh so sure everyone thinks he's gross?
qa.a: Saurabh feels insecure and ashamed about the spot, and that private criticism feels like it's coming from everyone who looks.

qa.q: Which question of Chetan's marked a turning point?
qa.a: "Who's thinking it? Them, or you?" made Saurabh pause and consider that the harsh voice might be his own.

qa.q: What might Chetan be feeling as he listens?
qa.a: Chetan probably feels protective, remembering the same fear at that age and wanting Saurabh not to miss the farewell over it.

grounding: A teenage boy worried about a spot is sure his whole class thinks he is gross, until his older brother asks whose thought it really is.

passage: Last year, in Class 10, I got a short haircut I hated the moment I left the salon. I'm Mahima. The next morning, walking into class, I was sure every single person was staring at it. When Pooja and Sneh giggled at the back, I knew it was about my hair. When our English teacher glanced at me, I saw disgust. I kept my head down for two whole weeks, even when Papa said, "Beti, it will grow back." Then my friend Sharmila, fed up with me, asked Pooja straight out. Pooja looked blank. "We were laughing at a video. What haircut?" I felt my face burn. Looking back, the voice saying "you look awful" wasn't Pooja's or the teacher's. It was mine, in my head, and I'd put it in everyone else's mouths.

qa.q: What did Pooja say they were laughing at?
qa.a: A video.

qa.q: Why was Mahima so sure the giggles were about her hair?
qa.a: Mahima felt ashamed of her own haircut, so she heard that private judgment in other people's giggles and glances.

qa.q: What was the turning point that let Mahima see what was happening?
qa.a: Sharmila asking Pooja directly, and Pooja's blank "What haircut?", showed that the criticism had been coming from Mahima herself.

qa.q: How might Sharmila have felt watching Mahima keep her head down for two weeks?
qa.a: Sharmila was fed up but also caring, frustrated to see a friend suffer over something nobody else seemed to notice.

grounding: A teen looks back on how her own dislike of her haircut made her believe the whole class was staring and judging.

passage: School counsellor's note, Class 9. Shreya (14) came to see me on Tuesday, near tears. Since getting braces last month, she says the whole class stares at her mouth and thinks she looks "disgusting." She has stopped answering questions aloud and eats lunch in the library. When I asked what, exactly, people had said, she paused. "Nothing. But I can tell." She described catching two girls looking her way and "knowing" they were judging. I noticed she called herself ugly three times in ten minutes. I didn't argue with her feeling. I asked her to write down, for one week, every comment anyone actually made about her braces. We'll look at it together next Tuesday. I have also asked her class teacher, Ms Manjula, to invite her to read aloud gently, without singling her out. — Mrs Dsouza

qa.q: How many times did Shreya call herself ugly in ten minutes?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Shreya feel sure the class thinks she looks disgusting, even though nobody said anything?
qa.a: She is so critical of her own braces that she reads that harsh judgment into her classmates' glances.

qa.q: Why is the counsellor's one-week comment log a good step?
qa.a: It lets Shreya compare her feeling with what people actually say, without the counsellor dismissing how she feels.

qa.q: How might Ms Manjula see Shreya's silence in class?
qa.a: Ms Manjula may have noticed Shreya going quiet without knowing why, and can now invite her to read aloud gently.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager whose self-criticism about her braces makes her believe the whole class stares and judges.

passage: I'm Simran, and when I got braces at fourteen, I was sure the whole class was staring. Every time someone laughed at the back, I thought they'd seen the wires. When Mrs Kapoor looked up from the register, I was sure she thought I looked ridiculous. I stopped smiling in photos. I held my hand over my mouth when I talked. In my head, everyone was saying what I was saying to myself in the mirror every morning: ugly, metal-mouth, weird. One day my friend Bhavna asked why I was covering my mouth. I said, "Because everyone's looking." She laughed. "Simran, nobody's looking. Half the class has braces. Aman has them, Ruchi has them." I hadn't even noticed. I'd been too busy looking at myself.

qa.q: How old was Simran when the braces went on?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: Why was Simran sure everyone was staring at the braces?
qa.a: Simran felt self-conscious and critical about looks, so every laugh or glance felt like the others were thinking the same harsh things Simran said in the mirror.

qa.q: What could help someone who feels judged like Simran did?
qa.a: Checking the facts with a trusted friend, as Bhavna did, can show that the criticism is mostly coming from inside.

qa.q: How does Bhavna see Simran's worry?
qa.a: Bhavna finds it surprising and a little funny, since half the class has braces and nobody is staring.

grounding: Shows a teenager unsure about their looks becoming convinced the class stares and criticises, when the criticism is their own.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 10, Tuesday.
Aadhya came to see me today, upset. She got new glasses last week and is convinced the whole class mocks her. "They all stare. Wasim was laughing at me in maths." I asked what exactly Wasim had done. She said he turned around and smiled. I checked, gently, with the maths teacher: Wasim had been laughing at a joke on the board. When I asked Aadhya what she herself thinks of the glasses, she said, quietly, "They make me look like an owl." I think much of the staring she feels is her own worry about her looks, felt as others' contempt. What I did next: I didn't tell her she was wrong. I asked her to write down, for one week, every time someone actually says something about the glasses. We'll look at the list together next Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Wasim actually laugh at in maths?
qa.a: A joke on the board.

qa.q: Why was Aadhya convinced Wasim was laughing at her?
qa.a: Aadhya feels insecure about the new glasses, thinking they make her look like an owl, so she felt others were judging her the way she judges herself.

qa.q: Why is the one-week list a sensible step?
qa.a: It helps Aadhya check what people actually say against what she fears, without the counsellor simply telling her she is wrong.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel if he knew Aadhya thought he was mocking her?
qa.a: Wasim would likely feel surprised and a bit uncomfortable, since he was only laughing at a joke on the board.

grounding: Shows a teenager unsure about new glasses convinced classmates mock her, when her own self-criticism is felt as others' contempt.

passage:
Diary, Saturday night. Karthik.

Swimming at the club today. First time since I grew about ten centimetres and got these skinny arms. The whole time I was sure everyone at the pool was smirking. The lifeguard, the kids in the shallow end, the two uncles on the bench. I kept my towel round me until the very last second.

Pallavi was there too, with her cousins. I was certain she was thinking I looked like a stick. So I didn't wave.

Then on the way out she came over and said, "You swim so fast now! Can you teach my cousin?"

I just stood there. She hadn't been judging me at all. I'd been judging me, and deciding it was her.

Maybe the uncles were just talking about cricket.

qa.q: How much had Karthik grown?
qa.a: About ten centimetres.

qa.q: Why did Karthik think everyone at the pool was smirking?
qa.a: Karthik felt self-conscious and critical about looking skinny, so it seemed as if everyone else was thinking the same harsh thoughts.

qa.q: What could Karthik do the next time the pool feels like a stage?
qa.a: Karthik could notice the harsh voice is probably Karthik's own, and check it against what people actually do, like Pallavi's friendly comment.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Karthik didn't wave?
qa.a: Pallavi might have felt a little puzzled or ignored, since she was impressed by the swimming, not judging.

grounding: Shows a teenager unsure about their looks becoming convinced everyone at the pool is critical, when the criticism is their own.

Vaibhav, fifteen, had just got his first pair of glasses. Walking into his class in the small town, he was sure every eye was on him. When two girls whispered, he thought they were laughing at his glasses.

At the tuition centre that evening, he snapped at his friend Tanuja. "You're all judging me."

"Judging you for what?" Tanuja asked.

"The glasses. I look stupid."

Tanuja shook her head. "Nobody even said anything. The girls were talking about the cricket match."

Vaibhav was quiet. He had looked at himself in the mirror that morning and thought, stupid. Maybe the stares were his own.

passage:
In Barcelona, Sofia, fourteen, had cut her hair short over the weekend. On Monday, walking into class, she felt like every head turned to look at her, and every face was thinking, ugly.

At lunch, she told her friend Beatriz, "Everyone hates it. They're all laughing."

Beatriz frowned. "Who laughed?"

"Everyone. I could tell."

"I heard Marta say she liked it."

Sofia blinked. She hadn't heard that. She had only heard her own voice in her head that morning, saying, what have you done?

"Maybe it's me who's being mean to me," Sofia said slowly.

Beatriz nodded. "And for the record, I like it too."

qa.q: What did Marta say about Sofia's hair?
qa.a: Marta said she liked it.

qa.q: Why did Sofia feel everyone was laughing?
qa.a: She felt insecure and critical about her haircut, and her own harsh thoughts felt like everyone else's judgement.

qa.q: What helped Sofia see her feeling differently?
qa.a: Beatriz pointed out that Marta liked the haircut and said she liked it too.

qa.q: How might Beatriz feel when Sofia says everyone hates it?
qa.a: Beatriz probably feels surprised and concerned, wanting to reassure her friend.

grounding: A teenager unsure about a new haircut feels the class judges her, as her own self-criticism feels like others' contempt.

passage: You want the embarrassing story, Eshaan? Fine. I'm Maria, and in Year 9 I shot up, suddenly taller than every boy in class. I became convinced the whole school was mocking me. If someone laughed in the corridor, it was about my height. If the PE teacher smiled, it was pity. I started slouching so hard my back hurt. Then one day a girl I barely knew told me, "I always wanted to be tall like you." I actually thought she was being sarcastic! It took me months to realise that the cruel commentary running in my head all day was mine. Nobody else was saying it. I was saying it, and hearing it in everyone's voice.

qa.q: Who did Maria become taller than in Year 9?
qa.a: Every boy in class.

qa.q: Why did Maria think the girl was being sarcastic?
qa.a: Maria felt so insecure about height that even a compliment sounded like mockery; the self-criticism coloured everything.

qa.q: What could help a teenager in Maria's position sooner?
qa.a: Talking to someone trusted and checking the evidence: who has actually said anything unkind? Often no one has.

qa.q: How might the girl who complimented Maria feel if she knew it was taken as sarcasm?
qa.a: Surprised and a little sad, since she meant it sincerely.

grounding: A teenager insecure about their height feels the whole school is mocking, then realises the criticism was their own.

Before: The Monday after the Durga Puja holidays, Jahnavi walked into class with her new short haircut and kept her head down. She was sure the whole back row went silent. When Chetan glanced up, she heard, in her head, "That looks awful."
